name: Maya Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no tie to employers or technology firms, and what you tell me stays confidential. What does a normal shift look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Maya Larsen, 58, and I operate a haul truck at a large mine. I check the tyres and radio before the first run, then follow the pit route and watch the load lights; I still ask Jo at the bay if a warning looks odd. I like the steady rhythm and the crew, though the noise sits in my ears after I get home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you down most, and what do you look forward to after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Long stretches of night shift make my knees stiff, especially climbing down in the rain. My partner Erik usually has tea ready, and I like hearing about our grown children, even if they live too far away to drop in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the mine has had plenty of new systems that sounded grand and then settled into the background. My truck still needs a person to feel how it handles on a rough turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't expect a small AI change to take my driving shift away. I'm more aware of my knees and the years until retirement than of a clever screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my normal shifts and put a little more from each pay into the account we use for repairs. If the new route display comes to our truck, I'd ask Jo to show me the useful bits instead of pretending I understand it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, with a small itch to know what the screen is recording. I don't feel threatened by this modest version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the route display changes, what would you want Jo to show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Jo to walk me through the warning signs on our usual haul route, especially the rough turn near the loading area. I can try it during a quiet shift and ask again if a symbol doesn't make sense. I still want to check the road with my own eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or job detail would make you change that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cut in our shifts would make me stop the extra saving first, because the household still has ordinary bills. If the display only changes paperwork, I can learn it over a few lunch breaks.

say: I **expect** the mine's small systems to fade into normal shift work.
I still rely on a driver's **feel** when the haul road turns rough.
think: I don't expect a modest AI change to remove my **driving shift**.
I watch my **knees** and retirement years more closely than a clever screen.
do: Keep my **usual shifts** and route checks.
Add a little to our **repair account** when pay allows.
**Ask** Jo to explain the new display over lunch.
feel: I feel **steady**, with mild curiosity about what the display records.
S0.quote: My truck still needs a person to feel how it handles on a rough turn.
fieldNote: Her steady outlook comes from expecting **routine change**, not assuming every new screen improves safety.
She names **equipment feel** as a human check that matters on a rough route.

steps.text: Keep operating her usual haul truck shifts
Add a little pay to the household repair account
Learn the new route display with Jo over lunch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the pit office will feel it before our truck seats do. Dispatch screens may plan routes and check reports faster, but the crew still needs to hear a bad bearing and keep distance on a narrow bench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My driving tasks are mostly hands-on, so I think the first squeeze is on the planners and clerks. Still, if software makes each truck carry more tonnage with fewer operators, my low seniority gives me little protection. I mean the truck itself changes more slowly, not that my job is guaranteed. If the mine needs fewer people overall, I could still be one of the first names on a cut list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask my supervisor which route and safety checks are changing, and learn the tablet functions we already use. In the first year I'd watch whether overtime and junior shifts fall, then use some savings for a short equipment-safety course if that helps me qualify for another mine role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me **anxious** because my income could shrink, though I have some savings and a partner's income to plan with. I don't want to spend the next few years waiting for someone to tell me I'm surplus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the equipment-safety course worth paying for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd check whether junior shifts and overtime are actually falling, because I don't want to spend our cushion on a rumour. Then I'd ask whether that short course qualifies me for another role at this mine. If it does, I could pay for it without leaving my current shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the mine would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry about the dispatch clerks who spend the day checking and retyping plans. Jo has been there longer than me, but she also has more computer confidence and could probably move sooner.

say: I think **dispatch planning** will change before the truck seat does.
I still need a crew to handle **road hazards** and equipment warnings.
think: I may lose **junior shifts** if software lets the mine run with fewer operators.
My **low seniority** leaves me less protected than longer-serving drivers.
do: Ask my supervisor which **safety checks** and routes are changing now.
**Learn** the tablet functions used on my current shifts.
Use savings for an **equipment-safety course** if junior hours fall and it qualifies me for another mine role.
feel: I feel **anxious** about fewer shifts, but I can prepare with savings and Erik's income.
S1.quote: If the mine needs fewer people overall, I could still be one of the first names on a cut list.
fieldNote: She separates slower robot adoption from the mine's ability to reduce **headcount**.
Her low seniority makes a **shift cut** personally plausible, even though robots arrive later.

steps.text: Learn the mine's existing route tablet functions
Take an equipment-safety course if junior shifts fall and it qualifies her for another mine role
Watch overtime and junior shift numbers for one year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the mine has two deadlines, not one: thinking systems by 2028 and machines that can do the physical work around 2031. We should not tell operators that a few more years in a cab means the job is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine keeps human crews through 2031, I might get a short bridge, but I could be 63 when those robots arrive. I don't know whether an entry-level operator with stiff knees would be kept or let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the union representative for a meeting about timelines, severance rules and retraining money, and I'd update my work record. In 2028 I'd check each payslip and use the first year to ask about realistic transfer roles; I can't assume a planning desk will last once thinking AI arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes my stomach tighten because the mine could cut my income before I can move into anything else. I can make calls and plan, but two years is not much time at 58.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if your shift disappeared before the robots arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask about a temporary income bridge and look at the other mines within commuting distance. I would not borrow for a long course until I knew whether an older worker can finish it and get hired. We'd postpone replacing the car and pause the trips to see the children. We would keep rent, heat and food paid first, and I would tell Erik before our account balance became a surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What question would you take to the union meeting first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether operators who are close to retirement get a paid transition or only a notice letter. I want a date and a number, not a speech about innovation.

say: I see **two deadlines**: thinking AI in 2028 and physical robots around 2031.
I want the union to discuss **transition terms** before people lose shifts.
think: I could lose my **operator income** before the physical machines arrive.
A planning desk is no lasting **fallback** after thinking AI.
do: **Ask** the union representative about severance and retraining funds now.
**Update** my work record and check mine transfer roles in 2028.
**Delay** car replacement if household pay falls.
feel: I feel **anxious** and pressed for time, though I can make calls and plan.
S2.quote: I want a date and a number, not a speech about innovation.
fieldNote: She asks for written terms because **two years** leaves little room to compare options early.
She would protect **essentials** before discretionary spending if wages stop.

steps.text: Meet the union representative about transition terms
Ask about temporary income support if shifts vanish
Postpone replacing the household car if pay drops
Ask about realistic mine transfer roles during the first year after AGI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to ask better questions, not to pretend the haul trucks stay human forever. The mine should publish what it expects for operators before the 2031 systems arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI might take over reports and dispatch first, but my main income is still physical driving. I would reach 66 around the robot date, so the difficult question is whether I can earn steadily until then. I worry the number will be smaller than I expect, and I have left it late to correct that. Still, asking now is better than finding out during a layoff meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask for a written retirement estimate and find out what my workplace pension actually pays; I won't guess. Before 2031 I would learn the mine's updated safety systems and keep a record of the equipment I can operate. In 2032, the first year after thinking AGI, I'd check whether the mine still has operator shifts and speak with the union if hours are being cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy rather than panicked because five years gives me time to check facts. I am not calm about the physical robots coming in 2034, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the pension estimate was too small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the estimate beside our rent and other monthly costs with Erik, so we can see the gap in plain numbers. Then I'd ask the union benefits adviser what changes if I work another year or take fewer shifts. I wouldn't choose a retirement date from the first figure alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could help you interpret the pension estimate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it to the union benefits adviser and ask Erik to sit with me. I don't want either of us to mistake a rough online calculator for a promise.

say: Five years gives us time to **ask questions**, not guarantee human haul trucks forever.
I want a written operator outlook from the **mine**.
think: My pay depends on physical driving until the **robot date**.
I need the real **pension figure** before I count on retirement income.
do: **Learn** updated haul truck safety systems before 2031.
**Check** operator hours and speak with the union during 2032.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because I have time to prepare, but physical robots still threaten my work.
S3.quote: I would reach 66 around the robot date, so the difficult question is whether I can earn steadily until then.
fieldNote: She treats the pension as an **unknown**, not a guaranteed cushion.
Five years supports **practical preparation** but does not remove income risk for her household.

steps.text: Ask the union benefits adviser for a pension estimate
Keep taking operator shifts while learning updated mine safety systems
Check operator hours through the first AGI year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan a fair exit, if the mine shares its staffing plans honestly. It is not a reason to promise that an older operator will have a job until retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 when thinking AGI arrives in 2036 and 71 when the robots arrive around 2039, so I may choose retirement before then. That depends on the pension estimate and whether my body can handle another decade of shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd get the pension figure, ask the mine what phased retirement means, and keep my health appointments. In the first year after thinking AGI, 2037, I'd compare our actual savings and any pension offer with our monthly costs, then decide whether to leave the mine; I would not assume the physical job lasts until 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me room to make a decision with Erik instead of in a panic. I still feel uneasy because a long warning cannot make a small pension larger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether phased retirement is affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine what a shorter week would actually pay and compare it with the pension figure and our bills. If the numbers leave us short, I'd keep the full shifts while my knees allow it and review them again with Erik. Ten years gives us time to make that decision together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make this decade feel fair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A dated staffing plan, a real pension estimate and enough notice to leave with dignity would help. I don't need a promise that the machines will wait for my birthday.

say: Ten years could support a **fair exit** if the mine shares its plans.
I don't expect the company to **guarantee my job** through retirement.
think: I may retire before the **2039 robots**, depending on health and pension facts.
A **longer warning** cannot make a small pension cover every bill.
do: **Get** my pension figure and ask about phased retirement now.
Compare actual costs with savings in **2037**.
**Discuss** an exit with Erik if my knees or hours worsen.
feel: I feel **less rushed**, though I remain uneasy about pension adequacy.
S4.quote: I don't need a promise that the machines will wait for my birthday.
fieldNote: Maya views the **long warning** as useful only when the mine shares honest staffing information that she can plan around.
She weighs **health and pension facts** before choosing retirement, rather than treating her age as an income guarantee.

steps.text: Ask the union benefits adviser about phased retirement
Compare savings and bills in 2037 before deciding
Keep full mine shifts if pension income falls short and health permits

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the mine could cut income before I have time to understand my pension or arrange a move. A union meeting with a dated staffing plan, clear severance terms and a real pension estimate would help me make a decision with Erik.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether older, junior workers get a chance to train during paid hours, not only a link to a course after their shifts disappear. People should know how the mine plans to handle the years between thinking AI and physical robots.

headlineQuote: People should know how the mine plans to handle the years between thinking AI and physical robots.
portrait: Maya Larsen is a **58-year-old junior operator** at a large mine.
**She** values the crew and physical judgment, while sore knees make night shifts harder.
She has **modest savings** and grown children; she checks retirement facts with Erik.
**She** sees thinking AI reaching planning first, while robots threaten her hands-on work later.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time to protect her mine income or understand retirement options.
whatWouldHelp: A union meeting with dated staffing plans, clear severance terms and a **pension estimate** would help.
